Loops, graphs, and more reliable AI agents

What if following the process wasn't up to the agent?

01 / 35

The familiar problem

“Done.”
According to whom?

The agent says it checked the facts.
The check never ran.
The next step happens anyway.

A prompt can describe a rule. The system needs to enforce it.

A process you can point at

The arrows are rules

Draft
→
Check
→
Approve

↳ Check fails → revise the draft → check again

Nodes do work. Arrows are permitted transitions.
Guards decide whether an arrow can be taken.

Foundations: W3C state machines · LangGraph Graph API

03 / 35

What moves through the graph

The graph remembers facts

Work

Draft version: B
Order facts: current
Validation: failed

Control

Repair attempts: 1 of 3
Approved version: none
Next step: repair

State is a record the controller can read. “I checked it” in the conversation is not the check result.

04 / 35

The anatomy of one arrow

A transition is a small contract

Transition contractRequired fact or outcome
Before · work identifiedThis draft and this recipient
Before · checks establishedValidation passed for this version
Before · permission establishedA person approved this version
After · action recordedStore delivery outcome; unknown means reconcile

The send service evaluates the guard when it executes the action.

05 / 35

Graph engineering

Old process ideas.
New kinds of workers.

State machines and workflows already describe steps, conditions, and recovery. Now some of those steps contain an AI agent.

“Graph engineering” is a growing umbrella. Here, we focus on controlling the workflow around the agent.

Context: LangChain: 3 Years of Graph Engineering · Feng et al., 2026 survey preprint

Unknown takes another arrow

Unknown → recover facts. Restored → validate again. Budget exhausted → person.

Recorded state · illustrative
Order serviceunavailable
Validationunknown
Budget2 waits left
Nextrecover facts

An unavailable service is not evidence of a bad draft—and never permission to send.

10 / 35

Customer reply · 4 / 4

A changed draft loses its clearance

A passed and was approved → edit creates B → validate and approve B.

Recorded state · illustrative
Current draftB
ApprovalA
Guardversions differ
Nextvalidate B

The system invalidates the old clearance. The agent cannot inherit it by saying the edit was small.

11 / 35

Fail closed

No evidence.
No permission to advance.

Check resultWorkflow response
PassAllow the next permitted step
FailRepair or reject
Unknown / check crashedBlock advancement; recover the evidence

A broken check must never silently count as a pass.

Security principle: OWASP: Fail Securely.

12 / 35

Loops need an exit

“Try again” needs a reason

What went wrong?What happens next?
Temporary tool outageWait, then retry within a budget
Bad outputRepair with feedback, then recheck
Send timed outFind out whether it sent before repeating
Attempts exhaustedStop and hand over to a person

A failed check changes the route. It doesn't lower the bar.

AWS: limit retries · Making retries safe

13 / 35

Room to think

Prescribe the boundaries.
Leave room inside them.

The agent chooses how

Explore, investigate, draft, compare, revise.

The system decides whether

Checks passed? Action allowed? Budget left? Approval current?

A whole agent can live inside one step. A graph with an AI choosing every arrow is still making AI choices.

Anthropic: Building effective agents · LangChain: Graph Engineering

14 / 35

Another useful graph shape

Parallel work still needs a join

One version → fact check + policy check + recipient check → join all required results.

“Fan out” starts independent work. “Fan in” gathers the required outcomes before deciding.

15 / 35

The join has its own guard

Two passes and a missing check

Required checkOutcome
FactsPass
PolicyPass
RecipientNo result returned

The join is blocked.

This is a completeness check, not a majority vote. Each required result needs an accountable outcome.

dev-loops · deterministic routing

One state, one next action

Current factsRouter response
Blocked or not authorizedStop
Waiting for an external resultWait / watch
Reviewer should act nextReview / fix route
“Ready” but current approval evidence missingReconcile the evidence
Merge ready but not authorizedWait for merge authorization

Read current facts first. Apply the routing rules in a defined order.

dev-loops · a bounded handoff

Give the worker a job card

What to work on

Target and current step
Required context
One bounded next action

What counts as finished

Acceptance criteria
Required evidence
Stop and permission boundaries

The handoff envelope is derived from resolved state and settings. A fresh worker gets the same task contract.

The envelope guides the worker; separate runtime checks enforce protected actions.

20 / 35

dev-loops · outer control, inner work

A loop can contain another loop

Observe → resolve → bounded action → refresh → observe. A bounded action may contain a review ↔ repair loop.

The outer loop chooses the next job. Inner loops do that job within their limits.

21 / 35

dev-loops · the review / repair loop

A review round has an output contract

Bundle → required review lenses → validate coverage and results. Missing → blocked. Complete → judge → act list. Actionable work → fix → fresh bundle; no blocking work → eligible for next gate.

Coverage, result validity, and judge disposition are separate checks. Only actionable findings go to the fixer.

22 / 35

This presentation · during preparation

We just used a UI sub-loop

Author edits → browser renders → automated checks and visual review → findings → author repairs → fresh render and checks.

One agent authored the deck. The parent agent reviewed screenshots. The shared browser suite checked fit, accessibility, and navigation.

Actual findings from the first expanded draft

The tests passed.
The graph still told the wrong story.

Hidden edge labelsShorten “draft ready” and “approved”
Wrong active routeKeep handover muted while budget remains
Crossed return lineMove the nested-loop callout off that path

Fit checks can establish that a diagram fits. A visual review checks whether its arrows make sense.

Turn the sub-loop into a reusable contract

Exit on evidence for the current render

RuleWhat it controls
Any edit → fresh renderOld screenshots cannot clear new HTML
Checks + visual review completeNo missing result silently counts as pass
Actionable finding → author repairRepeat the affected sub-loop, then recheck
Budget exhausted → human decisionProposed stop rule; not configured in this run

The outer workflow waits for this result, then refreshes. “Clean” means within the stated checks and review scope.

Waiting survives the conversation

Record the waitwork + revision + reason
→
External result arrivescheck or review
→
Refresh and routecurrent state wins

A checkpoint helps the next session reattach. It is a starting point for fresh checks, not permission to reuse stale conclusions.

Quiet waiting is not failure. Changed or contradictory state needs reconciliation.

30 / 35

The guarded routes

A pause can be the correct result

SnapshotAllowed next step
A · Unknown checkRecover evidence within a budget
B · Changed draftValidate and approve the current version
C · Missing authorityWait for an authorized decision

The goal is justified progress. “Keep going” is not always progress.

31 / 35

What this can promise

Predictable rules.
Fallible work.

With the same validated state and rules, code can choose the same permitted next step.

The agent can still write a wrong answer. A check can miss it. The workflow itself can be wrong.

Passing a gate establishes what that gate tested.

32 / 35

Make reliability a question you can test

Test the wrong turns

Deliberately introduceObserve
A failed or missing checkDoes advancement stop?
Changed work after approvalDoes stale evidence get rejected?
A timeout after an actionDoes recovery avoid duplicate effects?
The same task, many timesSuccess, escapes, handovers, time, cost

Evaluation approach: Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents.

33 / 35

Finding the flow

Make the next step
depend on evidence.

Draw one real process.
Mark what must be true before it advances.
Add the return paths—and the stops.

Let reliable results depend less on the agent following oh-so-sophisticated prompts.
